title: 🏜️ Sahrad — Second Age River Kingdoms, Drought & Reforms
rawNotionMarkup: Sahrad • Second Age Years 1–1,437 in Avarran retrospective dating. Sahrad's local eras, reign counts and cultural historical names are still undecided. This new chronicle deepens river, savanna, caravan, coast and desert societies. No modern Sultanate or royal line is automatically dated to the Second Age. ## The first broken channels (Years 1–135) After the Great Cataclysm ended the undocumented First Age, certain lunar works governing water and navigation became unreliable. This was catastrophic in some settlements dependent on them, but no two valleys were required to fail the same way. On a section of the Sahradi River, villages remembered the Dry Steps, a sequence of seasons when canal levels no longer matched predictions. Farmers dug emergency bypasses while wealthy households purchased rights to functioning wells. At the Stone Jar Landing, an independent town council forced sellers to mark the water they sold by ordinary measured volumes rather than by magical promises alone. An Elephantfolk waterwright, Ammara of the Deep Gauge, and a Human surveyor, Meret Saref, collected flood marks and hand-drawn channel charts. Their work, preserved in the Book of Unfaithful Wells, described failures openly without pretending to restore First Age texts. Some city officials destroyed copies, embarrassed by proof they had sold water they could not guarantee. Village children and itinerant potters recopied the markings on ordinary clay; this is one reason the work survives in incomplete later copies. In the broad savannas, Centaur households disagreed about seasonal pasture claims, while Lionfolk and Minotaur town councils argued over who could cross communal reserves during drought. A few disputes became violent; others ended in paid access, negotiated seasonal movement or joint watch parties. No continent-spanning animal-people monarchy resulted. ## The Brass-Well Kingdom (Years 136–321) A regional Brass-Well Kingdom, centered on a chain of river settlements and caravan junctions, rose through management of water allotments, salt trade and grain prices. Its ruler King Issaret the Patient ordered the making of public well records and built mundane reservoirs. His successor Queen Naluma of the Sealed Courtyard invested in moon magic that worked splendidly in a few gardens, yet allowed creditors to hold indebted farmers to life-consuming labor contracts. The scandal remembered as the Waterkeeper's Chains began when a group of rural households showed that their entire harvest had been pledged repeatedly against the same unpaid canal repairs. Workers sabotaged a tax register; soldiers retaliated by taking relatives hostage. A coalition of Elephantfolk accountants, Human laborers, Lionfolk advocates and Goblin caravan clerks petitioned royal magistrates. The resulting Open Well Decree made some emergency drinking water exempt from debt seizure. It did not abolish class hierarchy or end all bondage. Former hostages were not simply restored to their old lives; several later founded the Quiet Reed House, an independent refuge with no requirement of royal allegiance. In southern marshlands and coastal deltas, Merfolk and river port communities measured separate risks. Surface rulers coveted privileged underwater routes and sought restrictive contracts; several Merfolk councils refused them. Others traded voluntarily, often negotiating from strong independent positions. ## Prosperity and its shadows (Years 322–590) New lunar-derived arts enriched navigation, irrigation, agriculture and medicine. Sahrad's House of Five Bowls, a scholarly hospital and teaching network established across several cities, became known for combining practical diet, sanitation, nonmagical care and careful observation with newly reliable lunar healing. Its training halls admitted pupils from different peoples but charged fees that excluded many rural families. A Lionfolk healer, Yashel Varn, established a free courtyard for apprentices who agreed to teach outside the capital afterward. The charity struggled to survive and relied on donations from merchants who expected favorable public honors. The Brass-Well Kingdom's later rulers were weakened by succession disputes and water shortages. Some towns became independent; others accepted governors from new powers. The kingdom was not transformed automatically into the later Blue-Jar Crown (which belongs to the final 116 years) or the present Southern Sultanates. Differences in architecture and inheritance law persisted after political change. ### Savanna courts and wandering law A loose Circle of Grazing Stones linked independent Centaur communities and nearby pastoral and farming settlements around routes, sacred gathering places and water rights. In some circles, a mobile delegate could challenge the decision of a permanent landholder; elsewhere hereditary chiefs dismissed such claims. Speaker Denna of the Wide Crossing, a Centaur mediator, prevented one grazing dispute from becoming a much larger war by guaranteeing alternative seasonal access. Her agreements were negotiated, local and vulnerable to later violations. ## The Saffron Gate Disputes (Years 591–790) A competing inland caravan polity, the Saffron Gate Dominion, grew wealthy by licensing passage between wells and taxing luxury spices and ordinary water alike. Its governor Sethen of the Closed Hand turned debt failure into hereditary servitude on several roads. This policy produced forced migrations, banditry and resistance. The War of the Scattered Seals was a limited conflict among caravan city governments and resistant corridor towns. Soldiers burned storage yards; displaced families lost their tools and names were erased from some official records. This was not the Second Age's end, not an Orc campaign and not a war with the isolated Southern Wastes mages, who had not yet gathered. The most notable resistance came from the Unsealed Caravan, an alliance of merchants, freed workers, caravan guides and water carriers. An Elephantfolk legal instructor, Veshara Nul, drew up the Free-Water Claim, insisting that emergency drinking water could not be pledged as property. The Dominion called the claim rebellion; a few towns adopted it after difficult bargaining. It freed some families and brought reprisals against others. The caravan endured as a name for practical mutual aid, not a single bloodline or tribe. ## The long arguments of Wonder (Years 791–1,115) Not every city was drawn into the Dominion's conflicts. Independent savanna and coastal realms supported art, mathematics, temple scholarship, song, medicine and international trade; others financed magnificent observatories while neglecting sanitation. One coastal Hall of Contradictory Stars taught astronomers to record mutually inconsistent moon sightings rather than force them into a neat divine system. Priests from different cults, skeptical navigators and Fae interpreters argued heatedly there. Its collections were Second Age observations and not proof of authentic First Age records. In urban Lionfolk neighborhoods, some schools favored public service, others aristocratic honor and still others quiet domestic obligation. Minotaur advocates disagreed about whether a city's justice should be enforced by strong guardians or independent judges. Elephantfolk households included scholars, craftworkers and political reformers alongside waterwrights; no shared instinct for perfect memory was assumed. Pigfolk cooks, Cowfolk farmers and Foxfolk market families could achieve status, suffer discrimination or become officials in individual towns. Merfolk coastal enclaves retained their own trade policy and civic institutions. ## Late Wonder: the Tenth Granary Trial (Years 1,116–1,321) An unusually costly urban grain project became famous as the Tenth Granary. It promised stores protected by powerful new lunar methods; its sponsors neglected ordinary pest control, structural checks and equitable distribution. A badly managed season caused spoilage and hunger among tenant districts while the elite's stores remained intact. Rather than conceal the failure, Inspector Adira the Ledger-Keeper, a Human magistrate, released the failed inventory and requested testimony from workers whose warnings had been ignored. Witnesses faced threats and several fled, but the evidence brought the Open Storage Hearings, which required manual inspections and public granary accounting in participating towns. The reform was imperfect and local, yet a generation later it saved lives when another stored crop failed. Religious movements about generosity and water purity flourished alongside severe temple tolls and splinter sects. No single deity, new universal lunar source or continent-wide conversion is specified. This history preserves both real repression and everyday joys of gardens, marriages, markets and festivals that continued despite it. ## The last 116 years and the Age's end The Blue-Jar Crown, its water-rights hearings and Dispute of the Seventh Gate belong to the existing Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437) as a later regional state; this text does not identify it with the Brass-Well Kingdom or the Saffron Gate Dominion. At the end of Year 1,437, the earthquakes devastated communities around the world and ended the Second Age. Exact Sahradi losses and the protective magic's workings remain unresolved; no species was wiped out. Nor did Sahrad itself become the Southern Wastes: those magically formed in southeastern Avarra.
